statement: A rectangle of paper measures 9 cm by 4 cm. It is cut into pieces, and all the pieces are fitted together, with no gaps and no overlaps, to make a square. How long is each side of the square?

choices.misconception: I kept the perimeter the same, 26 cm, and divided it by 4, but cutting and rearranging keeps the area, not the perimeter.
I thought the longest side stays the same when the pieces are only moved around.
I added the length and the width, 9 + 4, as if that gave the side of the square.
I found the area, 36 square centimetres, and gave that number instead of the side length.

hints: What stays the same when pieces are only moved around?
Cutting and rearranging never changes the total area, although the perimeter can change. Find the area first, then the square with that area.
The area is $9 \times 4 = 36$ square centimetres. Which number times itself makes 36?

solutions.reliable: Moving pieces around without gaps or overlaps keeps the total area. The rectangle has area $9 \times 4 = 36\ \text{cm}^2$, so the square also has area $36\ \text{cm}^2$. Since $6 \times 6 = 36$, each side is 6 cm. Notice that the perimeter changed, from 26 cm to 24 cm. The transferable idea: rearranging pieces keeps the area, not the perimeter.

whyOnTest: Dissection problems test that area survives cutting and rearranging while perimeter does not.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
